newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ tourism slows in 1996, investors cautioned.
newsitem.headline: NZ tourism slows in 1996, investors cautioned.

text.p: The New Zealand tourism industry experienced a general slowdown over the last nine months, chartered accountants Ernst & Young said in a Tourism Sector Review released on Friday.
Terry Ngan, national director of Ernst & Young's Tourism and Leisure Consulting Group, said profitability in the New Zealand tourism industry appeared to have softened in 1996 compared to 1995.
* a drop in the growth rate of overseas holiday visitors;
* shorter lengths of stay due to change of visitor mix;
* lower domestic tourism due partly to increased trans-Tasman airline competition;
* the continuing strength of the New Zealand dollar compared to currencies in New Zealand's major visitor countries; and
Most publicly listed tourism companies had suffered profit drops in the last 12 months and Ernst and Young warned investors to research the industry thoroughly.
"We recommend caution for those contemplating entering the industry in the next 12 months and existing operators wanting to expand," said Ngan.
He said strong financial management and rational pricing policies would be critical in restraining any decline in profitability over the next 12 months.
Ernst & Young stood by its prediction of an eight percent average annual increase in overseas visitors until the year 2000, with 2.1 million visitor arrivals in that year.
However, it forecast a lower growth rate projection of six or seven percent, depending on the performance of the industry in the next six months.

Ngan said domestic tourism, which contributed approximately 50 percent of the industry's total earnings, may continue in the next six months to be threatened by continuing trans-Tasman airfare competition, a further slowdown in the economy, the relative cost of internal transport and a strong New Zealand dollar, making offshore holidays relatively more attractive.
"A thorough understanding of the dynamics of the local hotel sector and tourism industry, especially the competitive situation, is essential," Ngan said.
He predicted hotel investors would continue to favour strongly New Zealand because of the upsurge in tourists expected from the America's Cup and Sydney Olympic Games.

Investment would be particularly focused on Auckland, where Ngan expected more than 1,000 new hotel rooms to open by the end of 1999, based on current projects under construction or due to start shortly.
